title: Job 29:1–10
context: Job again takes up his parable (29:1), beginning the final discourse that runs through chapter 31. After the poem on wisdom in chapter 28, he looks back with longing to the months of old, when God watched over him, when God’s lamp shone on his head and the friendship of God was in his tent, when the Almighty was still with him and his children were around him (29:2–5). He remembers abundance pictured as steps washed with butter and a rock pouring out oil (29:6), and the respect he received at the city gate, where young men withdrew, the aged stood, and princes and nobles fell silent (29:7–10). This is not boasting to be scolded. It is the remembered life against which the losses of chapter 30 are measured, and it leads toward the oath of clearance in chapter 31. The narrator had already called Job “blameless and upright” (1:1), and the LORD called him “my servant” (1:8). Both traditions read the unit as honest remembrance and grief over what has been lost.

verses.text: Job again took up his parable, and said,
verses.arminianNotes: “Job again took up his parable, and said.” Arminian readers note that Job resumes speaking at length, beginning a final discourse that runs through chapter 31. His voice is given full room as he looks back and then forward to his oath.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the formal introduction of Job’s closing speech after the poem on wisdom in chapter 28. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as marking the start of Job’s last defense, which the book later closes with “The words of Job are ended” (31:40).

verses.text: “Oh that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me;
verses.arminianNotes: Job longs for the days “when God watched over me.” Arminian readers hear grief over a relationship that once felt close and protective. Job interprets his past blessing as God’s personal care, and he longs to have it again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a believer who once knew God’s watchful care and now feels its absence. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honest longing, recognizing that faithful people can experience seasons in which God’s care feels withdrawn.

verses.text: when his lamp shone on my head, and by his light I walked through darkness,
verses.arminianNotes: God’s lamp shone on Job’s head, and by his light Job walked through darkness. Arminian readers note the image of guidance and favor. In the past, God’s presence made even dark paths passable, which makes the present darkness harder.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the lamp as an image of God’s favor and guidance in Job’s former life. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s remembrance, and both note how the contrast with his present darkness deepens his lament in chapter 30.

verses.text: as I was in my prime, when the friendship of God was in my tent,
verses.arminianNotes: Job remembers his prime, “when the friendship of God was in my tent.” Arminian readers emphasize the relational language. Job does not only miss his wealth; he misses intimacy with God, which he feels has been lost.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see that Job’s deepest grief concerns communion with God, not merely possessions. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the heart of Job’s lament, his sense of lost fellowship, and both treat it with pastoral seriousness.

verses.text: when the Almighty was yet with me, and my children were around me,
verses.arminianNotes: Job recalls the time “when the Almighty was yet with me, and my children were around me.” Arminian readers note the tender pairing of God’s presence and Job’s children. Both have been taken from him, and the memory adds weight to his sorrow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the pain of a father recalling children who died (1:18–19). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with compassion, recognizing that Job’s grief for his children and his sense of God’s absence are bound together.

verses.text: when my steps were washed with butter, and the rock poured out streams of oil for me,
verses.arminianNotes: His steps were “washed with butter,” and the rock poured out oil. Arminian readers read these as poetic images of overflowing abundance. They are not literal descriptions but a vivid way of saying that life once seemed rich and easy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the images as hyperbole for prosperity and blessing. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetry of remembered abundance, and neither builds doctrine on the details of butter and oil.

verses.text: when I went out to the city gate, when I prepared my seat in the street.
verses.arminianNotes: Job went out to the city gate and prepared his seat in the street. Arminian readers note the gate as the place of public counsel and judgment. Job once held a respected role in the life of his community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the gate as the place where elders gave counsel and decided cases. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing Job’s former public standing, which prepares for his account of justice and care in 29:12–17.

verses.text: The young men saw me and hid themselves. The aged rose up and stood.
verses.arminianNotes: The young men hid themselves, and the aged rose and stood. Arminian readers note the respect Job once commanded across generations. The memory stands in painful contrast with 30:1, where younger men now mock him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the scene as a picture of honor freely given. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as remembrance rather than boasting, and both notice how deliberately it is set against the mockery of 30:1–10.

verses.text: The princes refrained from talking, and laid their hand on their mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: The princes refrained from talking and laid their hands on their mouths. Arminian readers note the gesture of respectful silence. Even those in authority deferred to Job’s counsel when he arrived at the gate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the gesture as a sign of the esteem in which Job’s wisdom was held. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s portrait of his former standing, without treating it as self-praise to be rebuked.

verses.text: The voice of the nobles was hushed, and their tongue stuck to the roof of their mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: The voice of the nobles was hushed. Arminian readers see the climax of the scene at the gate. Job remembers a time when his words carried weight, which makes his present experience of being ignored and scorned all the more bitter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image of respectful silence completed. Shared ground: both traditions read 29:7–10 as Job’s memory of honor in the community, offered as the background for his lament and his oath, not as pride.
